data.title: Federal judge rules against Trump's 75-country visa ban
data.description:
A federal judge ruled against the Trump administration’s pause on issuing visas to immigrants from 75 countries on Friday. 

In a 61-page decision, U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas found that this policy was “contrary to law” and was “in excess” of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s legal authority. 

The visa pause order was announced by the Trump administration in January as part of its efforts to curb an influx of immigrants they argued would place a strain on U.S. safety net programs. 

Vargas, who was nominated by former President Joe Biden, noted in her ruling that this ban affected nearly 40 percent of the world’s countries, including Egypt, Afghanistan, Somalia, Haiti, Iran, Brazil and Russia. 

“We are working to ensure the generosity of the American people will no longer be abused,” the State Department wrote in a social media post at the time of this announcement.  

In her Friday ruling, the federal judge cited the Immigration Nationality Act (INA) provision that “categorically prohibits” consular officers from basing their decisions in the visa review process on nationality. 

“Consular officers are required to conduct an individualized assessment of applicants and to refuse visas only to those whom the consular officer finds ineligible. The Policy nonetheless directs consular officers to refuse eligible applicants. 

Additionally, Vargas noted that the INA confers consular officers’ exclusive authority over the visa application review process. 

“Through the Policy, Secretary Rubio nonetheless overrides consular discretion and decision-making and dictates whether immigrant visas shall be granted or denied,” the judge wrote. “The Policy is thus patently unlawful and must be vacated under the [Administrative Procedure Act].”

The National Immigration Law Center, one of the groups representing the plaintiffs in this case, called the ruling a “significant victory” in a Friday statement. 

“The court made clear that immigration laws cannot be used to justify discrimination,” said Joanna Cuevas Ingram, a senior staff attorney at the organization. “We are determined to ensure every person and family this ban harmed receives appropriate relief and will continue to hold this administration accountable to its obligations under the law.” 

The Hill has reached out to the White House and the Justice Department for comment.

The ruling is the latest blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to crack down on immigration. In June, a federal judge ruled against the administration’s decision to bar the processing of any immigration application from 39 countries, stalling requests for work permits, green cards and citizenship applications.

data.title: The US is using the wrong measure of pressure on Iran
data.description:
Earlier this month — days after calling off a planned military strike against Iran due to a supposed diplomatic breakthrough — President Trump blasted Iran’s leadership on Truth Social as “unbelievably duplicitous.”

For weeks, Washington and Tehran have remained locked in a diplomatic stalemate, with little indication that either side is prepared to compromise. Around the same time, CNN reported that a senior officer at U.S. Central Command circulated an unusual request to military analysts for “creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran.” 

These developments are more closely connected than they appear. The request is more than simply a search for new instruments of pressure. It reflects a deeper strategic problem. The U.S. possesses overwhelming military, economic and diplomatic power. Yet those advantages matter only if they change how Tehran evaluates its options.

For years, Iran has approached confrontation with the U.S. from a simple assumption: Patience improves leverage. American administrations change. Elections reshape political priorities. Public attention shifts. Economic pressures accumulate. From Tehran’s perspective, delaying negotiations is not passive behavior — it is an active bargaining strategy. 

Unlike the Islamic Republic, every American administration operates within a visible political calendar. Midterm elections, fuel prices, congressional politics and public opinion inevitably shape Washington’s room for maneuver. Tehran studies that political calendar as carefully as it studies American force posture. Whether those factors ultimately determine U.S. policy is almost beside the point. What matters is that Iran believes they eventually will. 

This helps explain why successive American administrations have struggled to translate military superiority into durable political outcomes. Washington has often measured pressure by the tools it employs — airstrikes, sanctions, deployments and diplomatic isolation. Tehran has measured something else entirely, which is, whether each passing month improved its negotiating position. 

America’s regional partners further complicate that calculation. Saudi Arabia has reportedly urged restraint. Other Gulf states continue balancing two competing objectives of weakening Iran while avoiding a prolonged regional war that threatens their economies and domestic stability. From Tehran’s perspective, these competing interests reinforce an important expectation — that the coalition confronting Iran will eventually place greater value on stability than sustained pressure.

Conventional instruments remain indispensable. Military pressure, sanctions and diplomacy are not the problem. The problem is assuming that applying more pressure automatically produces greater leverage. Pressure succeeds only when it changes an adversary’s expectations. 

Thomas Schelling made this point decades ago in “Arms and Influence.” Coercion succeeds not because it imposes costs, but because it changes an adversary’s calculations. The relevant question today is therefore not how much damage American policy inflicts on Iran, but whether Tehran still believes that waiting promises a better outcome than negotiating today.

That distinction should reshape how Washington evaluates its strategy. Every military operation, diplomatic initiative, sanctions package or regional agreement should be judged against one strategic question: Does it strengthen or weaken Tehran’s confidence that delay improves its position? If the answer is no, tactical success is unlikely to translate into political success.

History offers reason to challenge Iran’s assumptions. The 1973 oil embargo did not permanently weaken the U.S. It accelerated American adaptation through greater energy resilience, technological innovation and strategic diversification. Democracies often appear vulnerable because their debates are public and their politics are noisy. Yet they have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to absorb shocks, adapt and emerge strategically stronger than their adversaries expected.

By confusing political debate for strategic weakness, Iran’s leaders may be making the same mistake that many of America’s adversaries have made before.

The ultimate measure of American strategy is neither the number of targets destroyed, nor the severity of sanctions imposed. It is whether Tehran concludes that further delay no longer improves its prospects. Military power creates opportunity. Coercion succeeds only when it changes expectations. 

Until Iran’s leaders believe that waiting no longer works to their advantage, Washington risks winning battles without achieving its strategic objective 

Bradley Martin is the executive director of the Near East Center for Strategic Studies. Dr. Liram Koblentz-Stenzler is the head of the Global Extremism and Antisemitism Desk at the International Institute for Counter-Terrorism at Reichman University, Herzliya, and a visiting scholar at Brandeis University.

data.title: Iran says 'world approved our victory' over the US
data.description:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday the war between the U.S. and Iran should end because the world has accepted Tehran’s victory in this conflict. 

His comments, which were reported by state media, come ahead of new economic sanctions from the U.S. expected next week. 

“The entire world approved our victory and the U.S. is hated,” he said, according to the state-run IRNA News Agency.

President Trump announced Wednesday that his administration would unleash the “most crushing economic operation ever” against Iran amid ongoing negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. 

“Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — It all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post.

“This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat,” Trump continued. 

The trading passage, which carries around a fifth of the world’s oil consumption on a daily basis during peacetime, has been effectively closed due to Iranian counterstrikes and a U.S. naval blockade. 

Iran and Oman have joint jurisdiction over this critical waterway, but Trump has threatened to make the strait a U.S. territory amid these ongoing talks. 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to unveil details of the new economic sanctions on Monday. 

“It is a one-two punch. We have ​the blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” the secretary told ​CNBC on Thursday. “It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this ⁠regime.”   

Iranian Foreign Affairs Minister Abbas Araghchi decried these anticipated economic penalties on Thursday, suggesting they were a means for the Trump administration to distract from domestic concerns about the cost of living.

“The so-called “Economic D-Day” is a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs,” the Iranian official wrote on social media. “Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians. US economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide.”

data.title: 'This is my place of business' — cakes and coffee in an age of rage
data.description:
“This is my place of business.”

Those words from Jim Sheehan, owner of the Wydaho Roasters coffee shop in Driggs, Idaho, have sparked the latest controversy over the right of businesses to refuse service on the basis of religious or political views.

Sheehan has drawn national attention after throwing out a group of pro-life teenagers, calling them the equivalent of a Ku Klux Klan meeting in his shop. Sheehan clearly caters to those who want their lattes with an added shot of rage.

However, this and a number of other cases have exposed the hypocrisy of many regarding the service businesses must provide customers with opposing views. From cakes to coffee, shops remain ground zero for an age of rage.

Years ago, politicians and pundits rallied around the effort to force Jack Phillips, a cakeshop owner, to create cakes celebrating same-sex marriages. Phillips objected that it violated his religious beliefs. The case went all the way to the Supreme Court in what many of us hoped would be a final resolution of this conflict.

I had long criticized the framing of the case (and other similar cases) under the religious clauses rather than treating it as a simple matter of free speech. In the end, the Supreme Court punted in a frustrating 2018 decision.

In 2023, however, the Supreme Court delivered a major victory for free speech in 303 Creative v. Elenis. It ruled that Lorie Smith, a Christian website designer, could refuse to provide services for a same-sex marriage. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote that “the framers designed the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment to protect the ‘freedom to think as you will and to speak as you think.’ … They did so because they saw the freedom of speech ‘both as an end and as a means.'”

But notably, in cases like Masterpiece Cakeshop, Phillips insisted that he would always sell cakes to any couple, including same-sex couples. He only refused to make cakes specifically celebrating same-sex marriages, due to his religious views.

The case of Wydaho is different. Sheehan refused the same general accommodation offered to all customers because he opposes pro-life causes. In the confrontation, Sheehan declared that “in my world” pro-lifers are no different from the Ku Klux Klan.

“This is my place of business,” he declared. “I did a lot of work to get people on the ballot so women would have the right to choose in the state of Idaho, and this is something I do not support, nor does my wife, and it’s our business. So we have that choice.”

In my view, they do have that choice. Yet it must also be acknowledged what Sheehan is doing is far more extreme than what Phillips did in Masterpiece Cakeshop. He is not being asked to create a coffee concoction opposing abortion, like a Cafe Au Life specialty drink. He acknowledges that other groups might use the shop — he just does not want these teenagers to use it to support pro-life causes.

The same controversy arose the same week across the country in Virginia. In Alexandria, Fatana Karimi, owner of the Karimi Salon, threw out a woman after she revealed that she was Israeli. Jessica Walton posted an account of the encounter, and a video was later posted on social media.

In the video, the person identified as Karimi says that she declared on Instagram that she would not serve those who support Israel. (She also adds that she got Walton to sign a release for the video.)

The Virginia Human Rights Act states that businesses cannot engage in “unlawful discrimination in employment because of race, color, religion, ethnic or national origin, sex, pregnancy, childbirth or related medical conditions, age, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, or military status.” Karimi will likely argue she refused service not due to Walton’s religion or national origin, but due to her support for Israel — a political position.

The case is reminiscent of the abusive treatment afforded to Harvard Law Professor Alan Dershowitz at Martha’s Vineyard by a pierogi stand. He was also refused service over his political views.

The line between national origin and religious discrimination versus political discrimination can be tenuous and unclear. However, in the video, the owner states that it is her national identity that is causing the action: “Get out of my shop. I can’t provide service to an Israeli. It’s against my political beliefs. You need to leave immediately.”

Back in Idaho, Sheehan’s bizarre analogy to the KKK outraged many, to the point that he later apologized for it. However, it is fascinating that liberals are now celebrating the right to exclude others for political or religious reasons, even when they are not asked to engage in any expressive act or make any creative product that contravenes their beliefs.

If that is now the case, many owe individuals such as Phillips an apology for years of costly lawsuits, even after the Supreme Court gave him his first nominal victory.

Sheehan could be prosecuted if he were refusing general service or accommodations to the teenagers due to their race or religion. But he is refusing service on the basis of his own political views. Wydaho Roasters does not appear to want business from people who are pro-life, of whom there might be quite a few in Idaho. Karimi appears not to want either Israeli or possibly Jewish customers. It is a curious business plan to exclude such a large segment of the market, but some owners are sure to put their political views before their profits.

However, those on the left cannot have it both ways. They cannot reject the free speech rights of some owners to decline service while celebrating others’ refusal to do the same thing. None of this is likely to make society any more civil. No one wants a black eye to go with the red-eye espresso.

Of course, recognizing the free speech rights of an unhinged coffee shop owner does not require patronizing his establishment. Sheehan clearly does not want to serve pro-life citizens, and I expect the feeling is mutual.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.” He is a member of the USA Today Board of Contributors.

data.title: Newsom praises Trump Accounts, first lady foster-youth efforts
data.description:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) offered rare praise for the Trump administration on Friday, endorsing its investment account program for children and foster youth initiatives. 

During a press conference on his CalKIDS program — a similar state-level initiative — Newsom said he was “enthusiastic about encouraging people to get a Trump Account.”

“I think it’s incredibly important. It’s one of the best things [Trump’s] done,” he added. 

Newsom also commended Texas Sen. Ted Cruz’s (R) and New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker’s (D) work on this initiative. These accounts, which became available last month, include a $1,000 investment from the federal government for children born in Trump’s second term. 

“We’re here to encourage people to take advantage of this, to not fall prey to the politics or the cynicism or maybe even the fear that if I download a Trump Account, somehow that means something,” Newsom said. “It doesn’t. It just means something for your kid. 

“It’s not Trump’s money; it’s your child’s money,” he added. 

Newsom has made affordable childcare a key part of his administration, launching a free diaper program initiative earlier this year. The Democrat is publicly weighing a run for president in 2028 — a race in which affordability is expected to be a key issue. 

The governor also offered a glowing review of first lady Melania Trump’s “Fostering the Future” initiative when asked by a reporter on Friday about his thoughts on this program, which sought to bridge gaps for children living in foster care to participate in the Trump Account program. 

“Melania Trump deserves a lot of credit because this was one of the gaps with the Trump Accounts is … there [were] eligibility issues around custodial eligibility — meaning guardians, parents — so foster kids in many respects may fall through the cracks,” Newsom said. 

The Democrat said he enrolled California in this federal program after former Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey (R) called to ask why the blue state was not participating in this initiative. 

“I said, ‘I didn’t know about this, governor,’” Newsom recalled telling Ducey. “And so absolutely, not only are we going to sign up and make sure that our foster kids are eligible, but I just put in a request as part of the three-party negotiation with the legislature in the next two weeks, appropriations dollars to back up that commitment.”

data.title: Live updates: Carney suspends trade talks with US, Freedom 250 Grand Prix begins in Washington
data.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on social platform X that the country would be suspending its trade talks with the U.S., setting Trump’s 50 percent tariffs into motion.

“The U.S. intends to impose a 50% tariff on $28 billion of Canadian goods. Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and business,” Carney wrote in a statement Friday night.

The response comes after President Trump’s decision on Thursday night to pause the 50 percent tariffs for three days, saying the U.S. and Canada were finalizing a deal. But Carney believes the trade talks with the U.S. have “not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”

Back in Washington, the streets will be filled with the roars of professional motor sports this weekend as the IndyCar Series brings its high-speed show to the nation’s capital for the first time ever for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix.

The event, which spans two days, will close streets near the National Mall and downtown D.C., and marks a dramatic conclusion to the summer’s 250th anniversary celebrations.

Follow live below.

data.title: The right to worship shall not be infringed
data.description:
Synagogues are becoming recurring targets in America. Just days ago, Kabbalat Shabbat services at Central Synagogue in the heart of New York City were disrupted when a man violently assaulted a congregant and a security guard.  

Last November, at Park East Synagogue in Manhattan, congregants were greeted by roughly 200 protesters chanting “Globalize the intifada,” “Death to the IDF” and “We need to make them scared,” forcing synagogue attendees to face a torrent of antisemitic slurs and threats. Then, in May, the harassment returned. This time, demonstrators waved a Hezbollah flag and screamed “rapist” and “pedophile” at Jewish people simply trying to enter the synagogue.  

The fact that American houses of worship require police protection just to let its congregation through the door should alarm every American.   

The pattern goes beyond New York: in Los Angeles, a group of masked antisemitic protesters gathered outside Wilshire Boulevard Temple, shouting “baby killers” and “Zionist pigs” at those seeking to enter. Two protesters eventually were arrested, for battery and destruction of property, after forcing their way inside of the synagogue. 

These are not isolated incidents. They represent a dangerous escalation threatening the fundamental right to worship freely and safely.     

In 2025 alone, ADL documented dozens of protest-related antisemitic incidents and nearly 530 incidents of harassment at synagogues in the United States. While overall antisemitic incidents declined since the year prior, physical assaults reached record levels.

And the crisis extends beyond the Jewish community. An LDS church was besieged and burned to the ground last fall in Michigan, and in May, three people were killed protecting students and worshipers at San Diego’s largest mosque. Houses of worship across the U.S. increasingly are being turned into flashpoints for confrontation rather than havens for reflection and community.  

That’s why ADL worked to craft and build broad coalition support for the  bipartisan and bicameral Right to Worship Act, recently introduced in Congress by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Reps. Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.) and Brad Knott (R-N.C.).   

The Right to Worship Act would establish a 100-foot safe access zone around places of religious worship, prohibiting conduct intended to disrupt religious services or impede people from attending them.   

At its core, the Right to Worship Act protects two fundamental American values: religious freedom and free speech. It explicitly safeguards the right to peacefully protest and other forms of protected expression under the First Amendment while drawing a clear line when conduct prevents or disrupts the ability of congregants to attend services.   

This new law is necessary. Existing protections at the federal level do not adequately address non-violent conduct that nevertheless is intended to intimidate worshippers, obstruct their passage, or interfere with their First Amendment right to religious worship.   

The Right to Worship Act builds on growing momentum at the state and local level. Along with community partners, ADL led coalition efforts to secure the passage of safe worship zone bills in New York, Maryland and Arizona, and in March, the New York City Council passed buffer zone legislation with a veto-proof majority. We continue to advocate for pending legislation in California and Pennsylvania as lawmakers in multiple other states are actively advancing similar measures. Much of this progress has been built on ADL’s research, model legislation and advocacy, and it demonstrates that leaders across the country recognize what is at stake. 

The American people  overwhelmingly agree. Support for buffer zone protections outside houses of worship reaches 70 percent of registered New York voters, a state that has been at the center of this debate. This support transcends partisan divides: 73 percent of Democrats, 73 percent of Republicans and 63 percent of independents back these measures. Support is equally strong across faith communities, with 83 percent of Jews, 76 percent of Muslims and 72 percent of Christians supporting buffer zone protections. 

This broad interfaith and bipartisan coalition reflects a fundamental truth: the right to worship without fear is not a Jewish issue, a Christian issue or a Muslim issue. It is an American issue.   

The question before Congress is straightforward: Will we continue to subject worshippers to intimidation and fear as they simply try to enter houses of worship, or will we reaffirm our commitment to religious freedom as a cornerstone of American democracy?   

Federal action is needed now. State and local efforts, while important, cannot provide comprehensive, nationwide protection that only federal legislation can deliver. The Right to Worship Act complements existing laws while filling critical gaps, ensuring that all can exercise their constitutional right to worship freely. 

Jonathan Greenblatt is CEO and National Director of ADL (the Anti-Defamation League).

data.title: Canada rejects US terms for trade deal as 50 percent tariffs take effect
data.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled his country’s negotiators from trade talks with the U.S. on Friday evening, just hours before the Trump administration’s new round of tariffs were set to go into effect. 

This decision followed weeks of intense negotiations between the two nations over President Trump’s proposed 50 percent tariffs on over $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. 

These new tariffs — which were originally scheduled to go into effect on Wednesday — would impact a range of goods, including wine, hockey sticks, cement, plywood and more. The prime minister has said these new policies are in “direct violation” of the free trade agreement between the U.S., Mexico and Canada. 

Carney vowed to “match those tariffs dollar for dollar” in a statement released Friday evening on social media. He added that Canada’s government will present “additional measures” to support workers and business owners in the country in the coming days. 

While the prime minister noted Canadian negotiators made “significant progress” in recent weeks, he said this had “not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”

“As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa,” he said in his statement.

“They have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute,” Carney continued. “However, last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer slammed Canada over its decision to walk away from these discussions in a statement shared on his official social media page.

“Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” Greer wrote, calling this a “missed opportunity” for a partnership between the two nations.

Canada and the U.S. have historically enjoyed a close relationship, but the Trump administration’s aggressive efforts to broker new trade agreements that favor the U.S. have placed these ties to the test. 

Trump has repeatedly suggested that the U.S. cede its northern neighbor as a “51st state” and addressed Carney as the “future governor of Canada.”

Carney wrote that Canada’s negotiators in these tariff discussions have “worked in that context.”

“We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship,” Carney continued. “Our government understood, before many, that America is altering all its trade relationships. Putting tariffs on its closest allies and charging access for its vast market.”

data.title: 'Shocking' fake poll firm puts industry under the microscope: 'Unfortunately not surprising'
data.description:
The revelation that two polls released in recent weeks from a purported polling firm were faked is adding a new curveball for a polling industry already trying to improve public trust in its work. 

Median Strategies made the stunning announcement earlier this past week that its poll results of the Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary and the Los Angeles mayoral race were not real and instead were put out as part of a “social experiment.” It said they should not be cited or treated as legitimate data.

Coming off well-publicized polling misses in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary and the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, the timing of the ploy wasn’t helpful either. 

Pollsters said this incident emphasizes the due diligence that media outlets and the public must conduct when looking at and trying to understand numbers being released. 

“It was very shocking, but unfortunately not surprising,” Ben Leff, the CEO of the polling and survey research firm Verasight, said about Median’s fake polls. “I think the industry and media are used to probably polls that aren’t conducted very well in terms of rigorous methods or how they’re verifying respondents, but this was sort of the extreme of that, where everything was completely fake.” 

The polling industry has already been dealing for years with struggles to improve its credibility in the eyes of the public, with trust shaken by President Trump’s repeated outperformances in 2016, 2020 and 2024, to varying extents. 

But that has been at least based on good-faith efforts from pollsters trying to model what an election may look like the best they can. That’s a different situation from Median, which pollsters emphasized shouldn’t be considered part of the industry. 

Median first released a poll on the Los Angeles mayor’s race, a contest that hasn’t seen any major public polling conducted since the primary election in June. It showed Mayor Karen Bass (D) leading progressive City Council member Nithya Raman (D) by 12 points, a lead that Bass touted in a later-deleted post on the social platform X. 

After Median revealed the poll was fake, Bass’s campaign denounced it, with a spokesperson calling for any “bad faith attempts to influence elections” to be “investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” 

Raman’s campaign attacked Bass for promoting a “fake poll without properly vetting the source.” 

A second fake poll from Median showed Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong leading the state’s Democratic primary for governor by 20 points. The democratic socialist ultimately lost the primary earlier this month in a major upset. 

The poll’s result was largely in line with what several other polls from legitimate firms were indicating, though polling was limited in the primary race’s final weeks. 

The extent to which the poll influenced expectations, and potentially turnout in the race, is impossible to quantify, but the more immediate impact may be how polls are perceived as the country is gearing up for the critical midterm elections in November. 

Geoffrey Skelley, the chief elections analyst at Decision Desk HQ, noted the impact is different than if a major pollster was revealed to be falsifying data. But he said he understands how this could affect perception. 

“I understand why, say in the aftermath of 2016, people have that attitude,” he said. “That is concerning, that it sort of adds fuel to the fire of ‘The polls are worthless,’ ‘The polls are meaningless,’ ‘They’re not even real’-kind of conversation.” 

Median maintained on its website that it wanted to see what would happen if it put out fake polls. 

“Median Strategies was created as a short-term social experiment examining how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” its message read. 

Median did not return a request from The Hill for comment. 

The Guardian identified the source behind Median as 21-year-old Rahil Prakash, a recent college graduate. He said he was inspired by the polling miss in the Michigan Senate primary to see if fake polls could “penetrate the ecosystem” easily.

“I was a bit shocked, perhaps at how fast this sort of information can spread,” he said.

Prakash said he wanted to apologize to the Bass, Raman and Hong campaigns.

“And I hope it gives a really good lesson going forward in that we need to be very serious about these things and very serious in how, if one person can do this, what can a serious operation do in the future,” he said.

Experts expressed skepticism about Median’s claims about its motive, noting various political or financial incentives for the results. The rise of prediction markets in recent years gives another potential impact on this, as bettors place wagers on a wide range of questions, including on who will win an election. Prakash told The Guardian he placed no bets on the races.

Skelley said fake pollsters have put out results in the past intended to influence prediction markets and make money off the impacts. But they have generally not come off looking as legitimate as Median did, either not having a website or having a suspicious-looking one. 

Leff said the first step that media outlets and members of the public should do if they see a poll from a pollster they don’t recognize is check if the pollster is a member of the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative. 

He said the initiative is similar to the bar for attorneys and provides credentials to pollsters that are transparent about disclosing their methodologies in detail. 

He said a second step is looking for a detailed methodology statement provided to the public included in the poll’s release. That statement would include information such as the number of respondents, margin of error and how respondents were recruited. 

Leff said Median had a “top-line” report of its methodology that didn’t provide a lot of details. 

“That was immediately a red flag to us,” he said. 

Of course, even a detailed methodology statement could still be faked, and conducting a deep dive may be more extensive than the average person knows to do or takes the time for. 

John Cluverius, the director of survey research for the UMass Lowell Center for Public Opinion, said this underscores the importance of not giving too much emphasis to any single poll but what pictures various polls from different pollsters are painting. 

“Thinking about polls in terms of them being different snapshots that are trying to measure the same thing, I think that’s very useful,” he said. 

Cluverius said he believes media outlets have become “smarter” about insisting on transparency from polling firms, becoming more selective in which polls they cover and don’t, which can help weed out those that are faulty. 

Leff noted this is just one of the threats the polling industry faces, pointing to bots and artificial intelligence that attempt to take surveys. 

In another incident, the polling aggregator FiftyPlusOne announced Thursday that it would “permanently ban” one polling firm and suspend another over a lack of disclosure that Florida GOP gubernatorial candidate James Fishback’s campaign was funding them. The banned firm was also accused of fabricating data, a claim that it denies. 

Ryan O’Donnell, the executive director of the left-leaning pollster Data for Progress, said the takeaway from the controversy needs to be more vigilance. 

“The lesson here isn’t that we should stop trusting polling — understanding public opinion is vital to a functioning democracy and there are plenty of credible, trustworthy pollsters out there,” he said. “People just need to know what to look for.”

Sarah Fortinsky contributed.

data.title: 5 things to know about the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington
data.description:
The streets of Washington will be filled with the roars of professional motor sports this weekend as the IndyCar Series brings its high-speed show to the nation’s capital for the first time ever during the final stretch of its 2026 season. 

The event, which spans two days and will close streets around the National Mall and downtown D.C., is being billed as one of the final spectacles commemorating the country’s 250th birthday at the behest of President Trump.  

Here’s everything you need to know ahead of Sunday’s Grand Prix in D.C. 

Race is punctuation mark on Freedom 250  

Sunday’s race will mark a dramatic conclusion to a summer in D.C. that came with a slew of major sports and cultural events presided over by Trump’s administration.  

The president hosted the Great American State Fair, facilitated a UFC primetime fight just outside the White House and delivered an address to the nation on July 4 before one of the largest fireworks displays downtown D.C. has seen.   

This weekend’s race was not on the initial 2026 IndyCar schedule, and it came at Trump’s behest.

Trump reportedly had been musing about a road race on D.C. streets for months, and in January, he directed the departments of Transportation and the Interior to designate a race route through the National Mall.  

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix will serve as the first auto race held on the streets of the nation’s capital, with organizers saying this week it will likely be a “one-and-done” event.  

Top Trump administration officials, like Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, are seeking to cast the event as a moment of unity for the country.  

“And I think if you look at the political divide in America, this is an event that brings America together,” Duffy told the New York Post this week. “Cars and racing is freedom and American.” 

Trump and first lady Melania Trump are expected to take a ceremonial lap around the course in “The Beast” on Sunday before the race starts, likely drawing even more attention to the unique end-of-summer showcase.  

IndyCar looking to create the right ‘visuals’  

The race for the IndyCar championship is entering its final stretch, and several of the sport’s top names will be racing this weekend in D.C.  

Series points leader Álex Palou will be in the field, along with top-ranked American Kyle Kirkwood, both of whom feature cars built by Honda Racing.   

The action starts Saturday with two practice races. Qualifying is set for that afternoon.  

Sunday’s race day activities will begin with a warmup at 9 a.m. before President Trump waves the green flag at 1 p.m.  

Those who follow the sport closely say Sunday’s spectacle will be a major moment for a racing league that has catered largely to a niche audience for decades.  

“It’s all about the visual for me. You know, time and place,” longtime motor sports journalist Curt Cavin wrote this week. “The visuals of the U.S. Capitol, Washington Monument, White House and the rest of the elements that make the city the most recognizable in the world will give the sport much-craved relevance. Everything else is secondary, including the actual race, which at close to three hours will be interesting in itself. Let’s see how cool all of this looks.”  

Race day will have a major impact on life in D.C. 

The buildout for Sunday’s race has been underway for weeks, closing city streets and making things difficult for commuters during a usually sleepy time of year in the district, when schools are closed and Congress is on recess.   

In addition to the 1.7-mile track featuring seven turns or 147 laps, IndyCar has put up massive hospitality suites, fenced off sidewalks on major downtown thoroughfares and left much of the usually busy National Mall unpassable to vehicle or pedestrian traffic during the tourist season.   

Local officials have been urging D.C. residents who do not plan to attend the race to stay away from the area all weekend, while those who do have tickets should seek public transportation to get to their designated viewing areas.   

“This is worse than cherry blossom,” D.C. commuter Nancy Marlow told local radio station WTOP this week, referencing the annual springtime festival that draws thousands to D.C.’s Tidal Basin. “I’ve been out here over an hour. This time of year, it normally takes me 20 minutes.” 

Other spots further from the racetrack have also been impacted, like the small streets near the Lincoln Memorial, which was closed briefly Friday while a promo for the race’s television coverage was being filmed.  

Critics raise noise concerns 

Anyone who has ever been to an IndyCar race knows the races are, if nothing else, loud and can cause the ground to shake.  

This has been a major point of concern for D.C. residents, business owners and operators of iconic district museums and art galleries that are either directly along the racetrack or not far away.  

In a letter sent to the National Park Service late last month, the nonprofit New Living Deal raised concern the race “may harm historic properties directly adjacent to the race course.”  

“Such vibrations are well above normal street traffic and even go beyond those of jackhammers, pile drivers, and even freight trains, which are commonly mitigated pieces of equipment during construction projects for noise as well as vibration due to their extremely high potential for impacts,” the nonprofit wrote. “Like many others across the nation, we question the necessity and cost of this event and seek clarity about the steps we assume are already being taken to mitigate adverse effects and harm to historic structures surrounding the proposed race course.”  

A spokesperson for the National Gallery of Art told WTOP it had conducted a vibration study in preparation for the race and put forth “a set of measures to ensure the safety of our staff, visitors, collection and facilities.” 

Race will pass key D.C. landmarks 

Spanning 1.7 miles, Sunday’s race will wind through some of D.C.’s most notable downtown streets and pass dozens of iconic landmarks and federal buildings. 

The start and finish line has been placed on 3rd Street NW between Pennsylvania and Maryland avenues, just blocks from the U.S. Capitol.  

Racers’ first turn will be west on Pennsylvania Avenue, where they will speed past the National Gallery of Art and National Archives before heading south on 9th Street NW past the Smithsonian.

The race track turns again on 7th Street NW through the heart of the National Mall, where the White House and Capitol will be most visible from inside a racer’s vehicle.  

The final stretch of the race will come along Independence Avenue SW, where drivers will head east before a sharp left turn at the National Museum of the American Indian and up 3rd Street NW toward the finish line and Delta 250 suites full of VIPs set to include President Trump.
